metadata.title: Amazon and McDonald’s just backed Uber—so why is the stock falling?

content.text:
Investing.com and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Investing.com — The fight for the delivery customer escalated in November. Amazon's move to give U.S. Prime members $0 delivery fees on Uber Eats orders sent DoorDash (NASDAQ:DASH) tumbling 9.4% on November 5, days before McDonald's named Uber its preferred delivery partner across 14 international markets. Yet Uber Technologies (NYSE:UBER)—the ride-hailing and delivery platform behind both partnerships—has slipped 5.9% over the past week to $65.60, leaving it down 4.8% over the past month.
The deal wins and 37% implied upside make Uber look like a bargain, but the share price is tracking a bottom line that is heading lower. Uber carries a "Great" Financial Health score, analysts forecast 11.2% revenue growth, and InvestingPro's valuation models flag the stock as "Undervalued" at $89.68. Yet consensus forecasts call for EPS to drop 28.2%, leaving shares at 38.7 times trailing earnings. Profit is falling back from a 2025 total that ran far above operating income, while driver incentives, autonomous-vehicle spending, and stock-based compensation keep costs climbing.
Identifying when a growing business is heading into a profit decline is what ProPicks AI is built for. In Top Value and Beat the S&P 500, two of InvestingPro's AI-driven stock strategies, Uber sits outside the November lineup: the models refused to absorb a 28% earnings contraction and hold large-cap leaders whose earnings are still growing.
The Membership Network That Keeps Customers Coming Back
Uber makes its money by running rides, restaurant meals, and grocery orders through a single app, and its membership program is what keeps customers inside it. Monthly active platform consumers reached a record 215 million in the third quarter, up 14% year-over-year, and Uber One climbed to roughly 55 million members, who now account for 70% of Delivery gross bookings. The network is still widening: grocery and retail delivery is running at a $15 billion annual rate, growing 40% year-over-year.
Third-quarter results confirmed the platform is still growing at scale. Adjusted EPS of $0.88 topped the $0.86 consensus, and revenue of $14.8 billion beat the $14.67 billion forecast. Gross bookings rose 20% to $59.82 billion—the fifth straight quarter of 20%-plus growth—with Delivery bookings up 22% to $28.54 billion and Mobility up 18% to $29.51 billion. Adjusted EBITDA expanded 31% to $2.96 billion.
That scale is turning into cash. Trailing 12-month free cash flow hit a record $10.4 billion, and management has been aggressively buying back shares.
Street Targets Point Up, Earnings Estimates Point Down
Wall Street is firmly in the bull camp. Goldman Sachs rates Uber a Buy at $110, UBS at $107, and Citi at $105, while Arete holds at $74. The median price target of $98.88 sits well above the share price, and even the Street's lowest target of $70.00 sits above it.
InvestingPro's Fair Value models make the bull case, placing intrinsic value at $89.68 per share—36.7% above the share price, but below the Street's $98.88 median target, making it the more conservative of the two.
The problem sits below the operating line. Trailing 12-month operating income climbed to $7.03 billion from $5.57 billion in fiscal 2025, yet net income to stockholders fell to $3.47 billion from $10.05 billion. Estimates are drifting lower too, with 12 analysts revising EPS forecasts down over the past 90 days.
The pressure on the operating side is building too, and much of it is hard to switch off. Driver supply shortfalls in Brazil and India forced costly incentive investments and left Mobility growth below management's own expectations. Stock-based compensation rose 27% to $591 million, widening the gap between GAAP and non-GAAP results. Uber has also committed $10 billion to autonomous-vehicle investment and will carry early vehicles on its own balance sheet, while total debt has climbed to $17.74 billion from $12.30 billion at the end of 2025.
Regulation and competition add to the strain. The EU Platform Work Directive and U.S. state-level gig worker rules could force drivers to be reclassified as employees—a direct hit to labor costs—and DoorDash's proposed $17 billion acquisition of Instacart (NASDAQ:CART) would give it roughly 19% of U.S. online grocery sales if it clears regulators.
Before buying into 37% implied upside, investors must weigh Uber's growing network against a bottom line that analysts expect to shrink. Autonomous-vehicle take-rate risks, driver supply costs, and free-cash-flow buyback pacing are detailed inside the Uber Technologies Pro Research Report.
Uber has built a consumer network that spans rides, restaurants, and groceries, and more of its customers are paying to stay inside it. Until reported profit stops shrinking and analysts stop cutting estimates, though, the low price reflects real earnings risk rather than a mispriced bargain.
Relying on a single platform stock while the delivery wars escalate leaves capital exposed to the profit downgrades that hit crowded trades first. Rather than attempting to separate real earnings growth from headline bargains manually, InvestingPro's data-driven strategies evaluate thousands of balance sheets every month to isolate large-cap companies whose profits are rising along with their sales.
